chief_complaint: sudden unprovoked spells of intense panic, palpitations, chest tightness, and fear of dying occurring multiple times weekly
hpi_details: 31F presents with 3-month history of sudden, unpredictable surges of overwhelming fear and panic reaching peak intensity within 10 minutes. During episodes, experiences racing heartbeat, shortness of breath, trembling, dizziness, and intense fear that she is having a heart attack or losing control. Episodes occur 3-4 times per week without specific situational triggers. Patient has developed persistent anticipatory anxiety regarding future attacks and avoids crowded grocery stores and elevators.
ideas: thinks she has a hidden cardiac arrhythmia that emergency room tests keep missing
concerns: terrified of having a panic attack in public where she cannot escape
expectations: wants fast-acting nerve pills to carry with her at all times
pmh: Multiple ED visits for chest pain (all cardiac workups including Holter monitor and stress test negative)

available_results.value: Sinus rhythm throughout reported symptomatic episodes; no clinically significant arrhythmia
No inducible ischemia or exercise-associated arrhythmia

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Panic Disorder is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes cognitive behavioral therapy and an SSRI or SNRI when medication is indicated, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden unprovoked spells of intense panic, palpitations, chest tightness, and fear of dying occurring multiple times weekly

Key HPI features: 31F presents with 3-month history of sudden, unpredictable surges of overwhelming fear and panic reaching peak intensity within 10 minutes. During episodes, experiences racing heartbeat, shortness of breath, trembling, dizziness, and intense fear that she is having a heart attack or losing control. Episodes occur 3-4 times per week without specific situational triggers. Patient has developed persistent anticipatory anxiety regarding future attacks and avoids crowded grocery stores and elevators.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals (baseline between attacks): HR 76, BP 118/76. Physical and neurological examinations unremarkable. Cardiac auscultation normal without murmurs or clicks. GAD-7 score 15. Thyroid function tests (TSH 1.4 uIU/mL) and ECG completely normal.
Relevant background/PMH: Multiple ED visits for chest pain (all cardiac workups including Holter monitor and stress test negative)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Panic Disorder.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Pheochromocytoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Agoraphobic homebound state.
management_principles: Education: validate symptoms while reinforcing benign physiological nature of adrenaline surges (breaking the fear-of-fear cycle)
If medication is indicated, consider an SSRI or SNRI after reviewing comorbidity, interactions, patient preference, and early activation risk

Psychotherapy: refer to Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) focusing on interoceptive exposure (deliberately inducing physical sensations like hyperventilation or spinning to habituate to somatic panic cues)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 31F presenting with recurrent unexpected panic attacks complicated by persistent anticipatory anxiety and agoraphobic avoidance.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals (baseline between attacks): HR 76, BP 118/76. Physical and neurological examinations unremarkable. Cardiac auscultation normal without murmurs or clicks. GAD-7 score 15. Thyroid function tests (TSH 1.4 uIU/mL) and ECG completely normal.
reference_soap.plan: Validate symptoms while explaining the panic cycle, while advising emergency evaluation for new, severe, persistent, or exertional chest pain, syncope, or other acute medical features. Refer for CBT with interoceptive and situational exposure. If medication is indicated, consider an SSRI or SNRI after reviewing comorbidity, interactions, patient preference, and early activation risk. Avoid chronic benzodiazepine maintenance.

learning_objectives: Recognize DSM-5 criteria for Panic Disorder (recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by >=1 month of anticipatory anxiety or maladaptive behavioral avoidance)
Differentiate Panic Disorder and Agoraphobia from medical phenocopies (hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, cardiac arrhythmias, caffeine/stimulant intoxication)
Implement interoceptive exposure principles within Cognitive Behavioral Therapy to extinguish somatic fear responses
Prescribe appropriate SSRI titration schedules for panic (starting at half standard depression doses to prevent initial somatic activation)

teaching.one_liner: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks accompanied by persistent concern about having future attacks.

must_ask.say: Do these intense spells of terror and heart racing strike out of nowhere?
During an attack, do you feel short of breath, chest tightness, or tingling in your hands?

must_ask.objective: Fear of dying or losing control
must_ask.say: Do you feel terrifying fear that you are having a heart attack or going crazy?
Are you constantly worrying about when the next attack might strike?
Do you avoid crowded places or public transport where escape might be difficult?

history.answer: I keep having these sudden, terrifying spells where my heart races, my chest tightens, and I honestly feel like I am about to die.
I worry constantly that something terrible is wrong with my heart, especially because these episodes strike completely without warning.
The first spell happened about 3 months ago, and lately they have been happening 3 to 4 times every week.
They hit me out of nowhere, surge to a peak within 10 minutes, and then slowly wind down over about 20 to 30 minutes.
During a spell, my heart pounds in my chest, I struggle to breathe, my hands shake, and I get dizzy and break into a sweat.
Yes, when an attack hits its worst point, I am convinced that I am having a heart attack or losing all control of my mind.
history.topic: Fear of dying or losing control

history.answer: I live in constant dread of the next attack, so I avoid elevators and crowded grocery stores where I feel trapped.
No, speaking in front of people or being evaluated at work doesn't bother me; these surges happen even when I am resting alone on my couch.
I do notice some tension in my shoulders and neck from being on edge, but the main issue is these sudden explosive spells.
It is severely limiting me because I have to map out my days around avoiding crowded spaces, and I have had to leave work early several times.
My work as an HR specialist has regular deadlines, but there haven't been any major personal, family, or financial crises.
No, I have never been through a traumatic event, and I don't have flashbacks, nightmares, or rituals I feel compelled to repeat.
I feel worn out and frustrated by this constant fear, but I do not feel depressed and I have never thought about ending my life.
No, my weight has been steady, and I haven't noticed heat intolerance, night sweats, or changes in bowel movements.
No, I have never passed out, and these spells never happen while I am exercising; they happen when I am resting.
I only have one cup of green tea in the morning, and I don't drink coffee or energy drinks at all.
I have a glass of wine perhaps once a month, and I have never taken sedatives, sleeping pills, or illicit drugs.
I try deep breathing or splashing cold water on my face, but once the surge starts rolling, nothing seems to help.
I really believe I have some hidden heart rhythm problem or heart defect that the emergency room tests keep missing.
I am terrified of having a full-blown attack in a crowded public place where I cannot escape or get emergency help.
I was hoping you could give me fast-acting nerve pills that I can carry in my purse at all times for when an attack starts.
I have visited the emergency room several times for chest pain, but all their ECGs, blood tests, a 24-hour Holter monitor, and a treadmill stress test were completely normal.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been admitted to a hospital overnight.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter remedies, or dietary supplements.
No, I do not have any allergies to medications or foods.
Nobody in my family has a history of sudden cardiac death, early heart attacks, or psychiatric disorders.
I work as a human resources specialist, live with my partner in an apartment, and I have never smoked cigarettes.
My last period was 2 weeks ago, my menstrual cycles are regular every 28 days, and there is no chance that I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Alert, neatly groomed, sitting upright with a tense posture and anxious facial expression, maintaining appropriate eye contact.
Fully oriented to person, place, and time; speech is fluent with normal rate and volume; mood is anxious with congruent affect; GAD-7 score is 15; no perceptual disturbances or suicidal ideation.
Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light; extraocular movements intact; no exophthalmos, lid lag, or scleral icterus.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, non-tender, moves freely with swallowing, and has no palpable nodules or audible bruits.
No resting or postural tremor noted in the outstretched fingers.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, rubs, or systolic clicks.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds and no wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial sensation and motor function.
Normal muscle bulk and tone throughout, with 5/5 motor strength symmetrically in all extremities.
